descriptions.title: Config-first: one file, sorted everywhere
descriptions.body: EasyFlow's design centre is a single configuration file, Tools/config.json — six tiers, their colors, 31 sub-labels, and ~185 sender/subject rules. Nothing downstream is hand-maintained: create_gmail_labels.py builds the colored Gmail label tree from it, create_filters.py compiles it into native Gmail filters, generate_apps_script() serializes it into the TIER_RULES object of a deployable Google Apps Script, and the browser extension loads the same shape to drive its rules engine and AI triage. Change the config once and every surface re-derives. save_config() always writes a .bak first, so an edit is never destructive.

descriptions.title: Three deployment surfaces, one engine
descriptions.body: The same tier model is delivered three ways so the user can pick their comfort level. (1) The browser extension is the hands-on path: open the Gmail side panel and classify on demand, with optional AI for the grey-area mail. (2) The Google Apps Script is the set-and-forget path: it runs on Google's servers every 15 minutes and triages stale mail nightly — the PC and browser can be off. (3) Native Gmail filters are the zero-software path: Gmail itself labels and files mail with nothing of EasyFlow's running at all. Most users combine the Apps Script for steady-state sorting with the extension for cleanup and review.

descriptions.title: Cross-browser OAuth (Chrome and Edge)
descriptions.body: Chrome exposes chrome.identity.getAuthToken backed by a 'Chrome app' OAuth client declared in the manifest — but Microsoft Edge does not support that API. getAuthToken() in the service worker probes the Chrome path once, and on an 'unsupported'/'Microsoft Edge' error transparently falls back to chrome.identity.launchWebAuthFlow against a separate 'Web application' OAuth client, caching the resulting token in storage (the web flow has no built-in cache). It remembers which method worked (_authMethod) so it never re-probes an unsupported API. This is what lets one codebase ship to both stores. OAuth scopes and client IDs are deliberately frozen — changing them would void the in-progress CASA verification.

descriptions.title: Resilient Gmail access (gmailFetch)
descriptions.body: MV3 service workers have no default fetch timeout, so a dropped Gmail response would hang forever with no error. gmailFetch wraps every call with an AbortController hard timeout (10s for GETs, 60s for destructive DELETE/batchModify), refreshes the token and retries once on 401, backs off exponentially on 429 (2/4/8s) and on network errors (2/4s, two retries), and treats Gmail's cascade-404 — returned when a parent label's children are deleted along with it — as a benign success rather than an error. This hardening is what makes bulk label and migration operations safe on large mailboxes.

descriptions.title: AI triage: bring-your-own-key, metadata-only
descriptions.body: AI is opt-in and never the default cost. The user picks one provider — Gemini, OpenAI, Anthropic, or a local Ollama model — and supplies their own key, stored in chrome.storage.local. aiTriageBatch() sends only the From header, Subject, and Gmail snippet (never the full body) to the model, asks for a {label, confidence} JSON, and then accepts the suggestion only if the returned label actually exists in the user's tier tree — a guard against the model inventing categories. A NO_TIERS pre-flight check and a tolerant response parser (which logs the raw text when it can't parse) keep the feature debuggable for non-technical users.

descriptions.title: Local desktop tool, not a server
descriptions.body: Unlike most QI projects, EasyFlow has no NSSM Windows service and no always-on backend. The Flask dashboard on port 8550 (within the project's 8550-8559 block) is a desktop convenience the owner runs only when designing tiers or generating artifacts; the registry classifies EasyFlow as a standalone_tool with family_tier standalone_tool. Once the Apps Script and filters are deployed, EasyFlow keeps sorting mail with nothing of its own running locally — the work has been pushed entirely to Google's infrastructure.

descriptions.title: Ten languages, by hand
descriptions.body: The UI ships in ten locales (EN default, plus ZH-CN, FR, DE, JA, KO, PT-BR, ES, HI, RU), maintained as Chrome _locales/ message catalogs plus three custom modules: i18n.js for UI strings, command-i18n.js for the side-panel commands, and guide-i18n.js for the onboarding walkthrough. Translation policy is manual-only — no machine/AI translation — and ~30 Tools/add_*_i18n.py helpers plus check_locales scripts keep every key present and in sync across all ten files. Arabic and other RTL languages are deferred to a future dedicated RTL edition to avoid layout rework mid-cycle.
